paras: In 1895 Ljubljana was hit by a strong earthquake. Many houses in the old town were damaged, and much of the city was rebuilt in the years that followed. But the face of the city that tourists photograph today was designed by one man: the architect Joze Plecnik.

Plecnik was born in Ljubljana in 1872. He worked in Vienna and in Prague, where parts of Prague Castle were renovated under his direction. In 1921 he came back home, and for more than thirty years he designed bridges, squares, a market and a library for his own city. The famous Triple Bridge is a good example. The stone bridge in the middle was built in 1842. Plecnik added two footbridges on the sides, and they were completed in 1932.

His work is everywhere along the riverbank. The Central Market, with its long line of columns, was designed by him, and the National and University Library, completed in 1941, is often called his masterpiece. In 2021 his work in Ljubljana was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list. Today his buildings are visited by thousands of people every day -- and most of them do not know his name.

listenings.text: Welcome to the Triple Bridge. Look down: the stone bridge in the middle was built in 1842. It was the only way across the river for almost ninety years. Then, in the 1930s, two footbridges were added, one on each side. They were designed by Joze Plecnik, the architect who changed the face of this city. Why three bridges? Because the old bridge was too narrow for all the people. Today it is used only by people walking, and in the evening it is the most beautiful place in Ljubljana.

I have sold vegetables at this market for thirty years, and my father sold them here before me. The building behind me, with all the columns, was designed by Plecnik too. It was built along the riverbank during the war, and it was finished in the 1940s. Tourists come to take photos of the columns. We come to work. Every morning fresh fruit and cheese are sold here, and in summer the market is full by eight. People ask me if it is a museum. I say no, it is a market. That is why it is still alive.
